title: Chapter 6: The Producer-Consumer Problem
description: Complete study of the Producer-Consumer problem: problem variations, AbstractBuffer framework, single-slot Buffer1a, circular buffer ambiguity, broken vs. mutex-protected BufferNa, optimized BufferN with passing-the-baton (passage de témoin), and Exercises 1–2.

sections.title: 1. Problem Variations, Framework & Single-Slot Buffer (Buffer1a)
sections.description: Variations, the 3 fundamental constraints, conceptual pseudo-code, AbstractBuffer<T>, and the 2-semaphore single-slot solution.

blocks.title: Problem Statement, Variations & Conceptual Pseudo-Code (Slides 3–8)
blocks.content:
Two types of threads must exchange data through a shared buffer (**tampon**): **producers** (writing items) and **consumers** (reading items).

### Problem Variations (Slides 3–5)
* **Buffer capacity:**
  * **Single-slot buffer** (`size = 1`): holds at most one item at a time.
  * **Multiple-slot buffer** (`size = N`, e.g. `size = 4`): holds up to $N$ items in FIFO order.
* **Thread multiplicity:**
  * **1 Producer / 1 Consumer (1P/1C)**
  * **$N$ Producers / $M$ Consumers (NP/MC)**

### The 3 Fundamental Constraints (Slide 6)
1. **Consume Once:** Every item placed in the buffer is consumed **only once** (*qu'une seule fois*).
2. **FIFO Order:** Items are consumed in the **exact order** in which they were produced.
3. **No Premature Overwrite:** If the buffer is full, a producer must wait until a slot is freed; if empty, a consumer must wait until an item is deposited.

### Conceptual Pseudo-Code (Slides 7–8)
* **Production:** wait until the buffer has space, deposit the item, signal the consumer.
* **Consumption:** wait until the buffer has content, withdraw the item, signal the producer.

```text
Producteur                          Consommateur
Depose(item) {                      item Preleve() {
  Tant que le tampon est plein:       Tant que le tampon est vide:
    Attendre                            Attendre
  Déposer l'item                      Retirer l'item
  Signaler ceci au consommateur       Signaler ceci au producteur
}                                   }
```

blocks.title: Single-Slot Buffer: Buffer1a<T> (Slides 12–13)

annotations.note: waitEmpty starts at 1 (buffer is initially empty); waitFull starts at 0. Invariant: waitEmpty + waitFull = 1.
Producer blocks until the slot is empty (waitEmpty == 1), consuming the empty-slot token.

blocks.title: Buffer1a Semaphore Invariant
blocks.front: In `Buffer1a<T>`, what are the initial values of `waitEmpty` and `waitFull`, and what invariant do they maintain?
blocks.back:
* `waitEmpty` starts at **1** (buffer is initially empty so a producer can enter).
* `waitFull` starts at **0** (consumers must wait for the first item).
* **Invariant:** `waitEmpty + waitFull = 1` (at most one thread accesses `element` at any moment, so no separate `mutex` is needed even with multiple producers/consumers).
blocks.hint: Think about what state the single slot starts in and whether a producer and consumer can ever be inside the critical region simultaneously.

blocks.question: In `Buffer1a<T>`, why is no separate `mutex` semaphore needed even if there are multiple producers and multiple consumers?
options: Because `waitEmpty + waitFull = 1`: at most one producer OR one consumer can be between `acquire()` and `release()` at any time.
Because `T element` is copied atomically by the CPU.
Because `PcoThread` automatically locks shared member variables.
Because `waitEmpty` is initialized to `size` instead of `1`.
blocks.correct_answer: Because `waitEmpty + waitFull = 1`: at most one producer OR one consumer can be between `acquire()` and `release()` at any time.
blocks.explanation: Since `waitEmpty` starts at 1 and `waitFull` starts at 0, only one thread can acquire a token before releasing the complementary token. Thus `element` is never accessed concurrently. (By contrast, in a multi-slot buffer of size N > 1, multiple tokens exist, so a `mutex` becomes necessary.)
hints: Count the total number of tokens circulating between `waitEmpty` and `waitFull`.
Can two producers both pass `waitEmpty.acquire()` before a consumer calls `waitEmpty.release()`?

sections.title: 2. Circular Buffer, Pointer Ambiguity & The Broken 2-Semaphore Attempt
sections.description: Modulo indexing, why writePointer == readPointer is ambiguous (Slide 17), and why BufferNa without mutex fails for N producers or M consumers.

blocks.title: Circular Buffer Indexing & The writePointer == readPointer Ambiguity (Slides 15–17)
blocks.content:
For a buffer of capacity $N$, we store items in a **circular array** with two indices initialized to `0`:
* `writePointer`: index where the next producer writes, then advances modulo $N$:
  ```cpp
  elements[writePointer] = item;
  writePointer = (writePointer + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
  ```
* `readPointer`: index where the next consumer reads, then advances modulo $N$:
  ```cpp
  item = elements[readPointer];
  readPointer = (readPointer + 1) % BUFFER_SIZE;
  ```

### Slide 17 Question: If `writePointer == readPointer`, is the buffer (1) Empty or (2) Full?
**It is ambiguous — it could be EITHER empty OR full!**
* Initially, `writePointer == 0` and `readPointer == 0` $\rightarrow$ the buffer is **empty**.
* If a producer writes $N$ items without any consumer reading, `writePointer` wraps around modulo $N$ back to `0 == readPointer` $\rightarrow$ the buffer is **full**.

### How `BufferNa` vs. `BufferN` Resolve the Ambiguity
* **`BufferNa`** resolves it **implicitly via semaphore counts**: `waitNotFull` (initialized to `size`) tracks free slots, and `waitNotEmpty` (initialized to `0`) tracks filled slots. The code never compares `writePointer` and `readPointer`.
* **`BufferN`** resolves it **explicitly via a counter variable `nbElements`** (initialized to `0`, protected by `mutex`): empty iff `nbElements == 0`, full iff `nbElements == bufferSize`.

blocks.title: 1st Broken Attempt: BufferNa Without mutex (Slides 18–20)

annotations.note: BUG (N > 1 producers): Two producers can both pass waitNotFull.acquire() when >= 2 slots are free and overwrite the same elements[writePointer]!
BUG: Concurrent read-modify-write on writePointer can lose an increment, leaving a slot uninitialized.
BUG (M > 1 consumers): Two consumers can both pass waitNotEmpty.acquire() when >= 2 items are present and read the exact same item!
BUG: Concurrent read-modify-write on readPointer can skip an item in the buffer.

blocks.title: Why the 2-Semaphore Attempt Works for 1P/1C but Breaks for NP/MC
blocks.content:
* **Why it works for 1 Producer / 1 Consumer (1P/1C):**
  * Only **one** thread ever reads or modifies `writePointer` and writes to `elements[writePointer]`.
  * Only **one** thread ever reads or modifies `readPointer` and reads `elements[readPointer]`.
  * `waitNotFull` and `waitNotEmpty` guarantee that the producer and consumer never access the same array slot simultaneously.
* **Why it breaks for $N$ Producers or $M$ Consumers (NP/MC):**
  * Suppose `size = 4` and the buffer is empty (`waitNotFull = 4`). Two producers $P_1$ and $P_2$ both call `waitNotFull.acquire()` and both succeed (`waitNotFull` drops to 2).
  * Both read `writePointer == 0`.
  * $P_1$ writes `elements[0] = item1`; $P_2$ overwrites `elements[0] = item2` (**lost item**!).
  * Both compute `(0 + 1) % 4` or race on incrementing `writePointer`, potentially advancing it to `2` while `elements[1]` was never written (**garbage read** by a consumer!).
  * Symmetrically, two consumers $C_1, C_2$ can both pass `waitNotEmpty.acquire()` and read the same `elements[readPointer]`, violating Constraint 1 (consume only once).

blocks.title: Circular Buffer Ambiguity
blocks.front: In a circular buffer of size $N$, if `writePointer == readPointer`, is the buffer empty or full? How do `BufferNa` and `BufferN` resolve this?
blocks.back:
**It is ambiguous** — `writePointer == readPointer` occurs both when the buffer is **empty** (e.g., initially at 0) and when it is **full** (after $N$ unconsumed writes wrap around).
* **`BufferNa`** avoids testing pointers altogether by tracking free/filled slots in `waitNotFull(size)` and `waitNotEmpty(0)`.
* **`BufferN`** tracks the exact occupancy in a dedicated `nbElements` counter.
blocks.hint: Think about what happens after 0 writes vs. N writes with 0 reads.

blocks.question: Under which configuration does the 2-semaphore `BufferNa` (without `mutex`) fail?
options: Whenever there are 2 or more producers OR 2 or more consumers (NP/MC).
Even with 1 producer and 1 consumer, because `writePointer` and `readPointer` collide.
Only when `bufferSize == 1`.
Only when the buffer becomes completely full.
blocks.correct_answer: Whenever there are 2 or more producers OR 2 or more consumers (NP/MC).
blocks.explanation: With 1P/1C, only one thread ever touches `writePointer` and only one ever touches `readPointer`, while `waitNotFull`/`waitNotEmpty` keep them off the same slot. With >= 2 producers (or >= 2 consumers), multiple threads can pass `waitNotFull.acquire()` (or `waitNotEmpty.acquire()`) simultaneously and race on `elements[writePointer]` and `writePointer` (or `readPointer`).
hints: Can two producers pass `waitNotFull.acquire()` at the same time when `bufferSize = 4`?
What happens if both producers read `writePointer == 0` before either increments it?

sections.title: 3. Correct N-Slot Buffer: BufferNa<T> (3 Semaphores)
sections.description: Adding a mutex semaphore to protect circular buffer state across N producers and M consumers.

blocks.title: BufferNa Synchronization Flow (3 Semaphores)
blocks.caption: BufferNa uses waitNotFull(size) and waitNotEmpty(0) for capacity/item counting, plus mutex(1) to protect writePointer, readPointer, and elements[].
blocks.source:
graph LR
  Prod["Producer: put(item)"] --> WNF["waitNotFull.acquire()"]
  WNF --> M1["mutex.acquire()"]
  M1 --> Write["elements[writePointer] = item\nwritePointer = (writePointer + 1) % size"]
  Write --> R1["waitNotEmpty.release()"]
  R1 --> U1["mutex.release()"]

  Cons["Consumer: get()"] --> WNE["waitNotEmpty.acquire()"]
  WNE --> M2["mutex.acquire()"]
  M2 --> Read["item = elements[readPointer]\nreadPointer = (readPointer + 1) % size"]
  Read --> R2["waitNotFull.release()"]
  R2 --> U2["mutex.release()"]
  classDef sem fill:#e0e7ff,stroke:#4f46e5,stroke-width:1.5px;
  class WNF,M1,R1,U1,WNE,M2,R2,U2 sem;

blocks.title: Complete Correct BufferNa<T> Class (Slides 21–22)

annotations.note: Three semaphores: mutex(1) for mutual exclusion, waitNotFull(size) for free slots, waitNotEmpty(0) for filled slots.
Wait for a free slot FIRST (before acquiring mutex) to avoid holding mutex while blocked!
Acquire mutex so only one thread updates writePointer and elements[] at a time.
Wait for an available item FIRST (before acquiring mutex).

blocks.title: BufferNa Semaphore Roles & Initial Values
blocks.front: What are the 3 semaphores in `BufferNa(unsigned int size)`, their initial values, and the order of `acquire()` calls?
blocks.back:
* `mutex(1)` — protects `elements[]`, `writePointer`, `readPointer`.
* `waitNotFull(size)` — counts free slots (blocks producers when 0).
* `waitNotEmpty(0)` — counts available items (blocks consumers when 0).

**Critical order:** `waitNotFull.acquire()` / `waitNotEmpty.acquire()` MUST come **before** `mutex.acquire()`, otherwise a blocked thread would hold `mutex` and cause a **deadlock**.
blocks.hint: What happens if a thread acquires mutex first and then blocks waiting for the buffer to become non-full?

sections.title: 4. Optimized BufferN<T> & Passing the Baton (Passage de Témoin)
sections.description: Reducing semaphore operations in the uncontended case using explicit waiting counters and passing-the-baton ownership transfer.

blocks.title: Complete Optimized BufferN<T> Class (Slides 23–25)

annotations.note: Uses `if` (NOT `while`) because baton passing guarantees the buffer is non-full when woken.
Woken producer does NOT call mutex.acquire() again — the consumer that called waitProd.release() kept mutex locked and handed ownership to it.
Signaler decrements nbWaitingConso while still holding mutex, before waking the consumer.
Passes the baton: calls waitConso.release() INSTEAD of mutex.release().
Symmetric baton reception in get(): consumer resumes inside the critical section without re-acquiring mutex.
Symmetric baton handoff to a waiting producer when nbWaitingProd > 0.

blocks.title: Passing the Baton (Passage de Témoin) Sequence
blocks.caption: Consumer C1 blocks when nbElements == 0. Producer P1 deposits an item, keeps mutex locked, decrements nbWaitingConso, and passes the baton directly to C1 via waitConso.release().
blocks.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C1 as Consumer C1
  participant M as mutex (init 1)
  participant WC as waitConso (init 0)
  participant P1 as Producer P1

  C1->>M: acquire() [mutex=0]
  Note over C1: nbElements == 0 -> nbWaitingConso = 1
  C1->>M: release() [mutex=1]
  C1->>WC: acquire() [blocks]

  P1->>M: acquire() [mutex=0]
  Note over P1: writes item, nbElements = 1
  Note over P1: nbWaitingConso > 0 -> nbWaitingConso = 0
  P1->>WC: release() [wakes C1, mutex stays 0!]
  Note over P1: P1 exits WITHOUT mutex.release()

  WC-->>C1: C1 resumes (holds baton!)
  Note over C1: reads item, nbElements = 0
  Note over C1: nbWaitingProd == 0
  C1->>M: release() [mutex=1]

blocks.title: Deep Dive: The 4 Subtleties of Passing the Baton (Passage de Témoin)
blocks.content:
`BufferN` uses the **Passing the Baton** (*passage de témoin*) pattern. Every detail of this pattern is coupled—changing any one breaks correctness:

1. **Why is `mutex` NOT released when `nbWaitingConso > 0` (or `nbWaitingProd > 0`)?**
   The exiting thread **transfers ownership** of the critical section directly to the woken thread. Because `mutex` stays at `0`, **no newcomer thread** can barge into `put()` or `get()` in between the `waitConso.release()` and the woken consumer resuming.
2. **Why does the woken thread NOT re-acquire `mutex` after `waitProd.acquire()` / `waitConso.acquire()`?**
   Because the signaler did **not** release `mutex`! The woken thread wakes up **already owning the logical lock** (`mutex == 0`). When it finishes its own work, *it* will either pass the baton to someone else or finally call `mutex.release()`.
3. **Why does `if` work instead of `while`?**
   With standard condition variables (Mesa semantics), a woken thread must re-check its condition in a `while` loop because a newcomer could steal the item/slot before the woken thread re-acquires the lock. Here, **no newcomer can enter** because `mutex` never became `1`! The condition (`nbElements > 0` for `get`, `nbElements < bufferSize` for `put`) is **guaranteed** to still hold when the woken thread resumes.
4. **Why is `nbWaiting*` decremented by the signaler under `mutex`?**
   `nbWaitingProd` and `nbWaitingConso` are shared state protected by `mutex`. Decrementing `nbWaitingConso -= 1` **before** calling `waitConso.release()` (while the signaler still holds `mutex`) ensures the count is exact at all times—if another thread later enters the critical section, it will never see a stale waiting count or issue a duplicate wakeup.

blocks.title: Passing the Baton: Why `if` Instead of `while`?
blocks.front: In `BufferN<T>`, why is `if (nbElements == 0)` sufficient instead of `while (nbElements == 0)`?
blocks.back: Because of **passing the baton** (*passage de témoin*): when a producer wakes a waiting consumer via `waitConso.release()`, it does **not** release `mutex`. Since `mutex` remains `0`, no other thread can enter the critical section and steal the item before the woken consumer runs, guaranteeing `nbElements > 0`.
blocks.hint: Could any other consumer sneak in between `waitConso.release()` and `waitConso.acquire()` returning?

blocks.title: Synthesis: What Breaks If You Release `mutex` Before `waitConso.release()` in `BufferN`?
blocks.prompt: Suppose a student modifies `BufferN::put()` so that it always calls `mutex.release()` AND `waitConso.release()` (and changes `get()` to re-acquire `mutex` after `waitConso.acquire()`). What bug does this introduce if `get()` still uses `if (nbElements == 0)`?
self_check_criteria: Identified that releasing `mutex` allows a newcomer consumer to enter `get()` before the woken consumer re-acquires `mutex`.
Explained that the newcomer consumer can consume the newly deposited item, bringing `nbElements` back to `0`.
Concluded that the woken consumer—using `if` instead of `while`—would skip re-checking `nbElements == 0` and read garbage from an empty buffer (and underflow `nbElements`!).
blocks.model_answer: If `mutex` is released before/alongside `waitConso.release()`, a fast newcomer consumer can acquire `mutex`, consume the single item (`nbElements` becomes 0), and exit. When the woken consumer finally acquires `mutex` after `waitConso.acquire()`, the `if (nbElements == 0)` check is NOT re-evaluated—it blindly reads `elements[readPointer]` from an empty buffer and decrements `nbElements` below 0. Without baton passing, you must use a `while` loop.

blocks.question: In `BufferN<T>::put()`, when `nbWaitingConso > 0` at the end of `put()`, what happens to `mutex`?
options: `mutex` is NOT released by `put()`; ownership of the critical section is passed to the woken consumer via `waitConso.release()`.
`mutex.release()` is called first, then `waitConso.release()`.
`waitConso.release()` is called, and the woken consumer immediately calls `mutex.acquire()`.
`mutex` is released twice: once by `put()` and once by the woken consumer.
blocks.correct_answer: `mutex` is NOT released by `put()`; ownership of the critical section is passed to the woken consumer via `waitConso.release()`.
blocks.explanation: That is the essence of *passage de témoin*: `put()` keeps `mutex` at 0 and wakes one waiting consumer on `waitConso`. The woken consumer resumes directly inside the critical section without calling `mutex.acquire()`, and will release `mutex` (or pass the baton again) when it finishes.
hints: Look at the `if (nbWaitingConso > 0) { ... } else { mutex.release(); }` branch in `BufferN::put()`.
Does the woken consumer call `mutex.acquire()` after `waitConso.acquire()`?

sections.title: 5. Comparison (BufferNa vs. BufferN) & Exercises 1–2
sections.description: Performance and complexity tradeoffs (Slide 26), swapping release/acquire order (Exercise 1, Slides 27–28), and splitting mutex (Exercise 2, Slide 29).

blocks.title: Comparison: BufferNa vs. BufferN (Slide 26)
blocks.content:
| Criterion | `BufferNa` (3 Semaphores) | `BufferN` (Passing the Baton) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Semaphore ops / call (uncontended)** | **Always 4** (`waitNotFull/Empty.acquire`, `mutex.acquire`, `waitNotEmpty/Full.release`, `mutex.release`) | **2** (`mutex.acquire`, `mutex.release`) when neither blocking nor waking |
| **Semaphore ops / call (contended)** | **4** (plus OS blocking on semaphore) | **4** (`mutex.acquire`, `mutex.release`, `wait*.acquire`, and either `wait*.release` or `mutex.release`) |
| **Code Complexity** | Simple, short, easy to verify | Higher complexity; relies on subtle baton-passing invariant |
| **Fairness / Barging** | Woken threads still compete for `mutex` with newcomers | Baton handoff gives the critical section directly to the woken thread (prevents newcomer barging) |
| **Can `mutex` be split?** | **Yes** (`mutexProd` + `mutexConso`) | **No** (both roles mutate `nbElements` and `nbWaiting*`) |

blocks.title: Exercise 1: Swapping mutex.release() and waitX.release() in BufferNa (Slides 27–28)

annotations.note: SAFE & SLIGHTLY BETTER: mutex is already free (1) when the consumer wakes up on line 7!
SAFE & SLIGHTLY BETTER: mutex is already free (1) when the producer wakes up on line 17!

blocks.title: Critical Analysis: Exercises 1 & 2 (Slides 27–29)
blocks.content:
### Exercise 1: Swapping `release()` vs. Swapping `acquire()` in `BufferNa` (Slides 27–28)
* **Can we swap the trailing `release()` calls (`mutex.release()` before `waitNotEmpty.release()`)?**
  **Yes — and it is actually slightly better!** If a consumer is waiting on `waitNotEmpty` and wakes up immediately when `waitNotEmpty.release()` runs, `mutex` is **already `1`**, avoiding an extra block/context-switch on `mutex.acquire()`.
* **Contrast — what if we swapped the leading `acquire()` calls (`mutex.acquire()` before `waitNotFull.acquire()`)?**
  **DEADLOCK!** If the buffer is full, a producer acquires `mutex` (setting `mutex = 0`) and then blocks on `waitNotFull.acquire()`. Now no consumer can ever acquire `mutex` to call `get()` and `waitNotFull.release()`, freezing the system forever.

### Exercise 2: Splitting `mutex` into `mutexProd` and `mutexConso` (Slide 29)
* **In `BufferNa`:** **Yes, it works!**
  Producers only read/modify `writePointer`, and consumers only read/modify `readPointer`. Meanwhile, `waitNotFull` and `waitNotEmpty` guarantee that a producer and a consumer never access the same array slot `elements[i]` simultaneously. Splitting `mutex` into `mutexProd(1)` and `mutexConso(1)` even **increases parallelism**, allowing one producer and one consumer to access different slots at the same time.
* **In `BufferN` (optimized):** **No, it breaks!**
  Both producers and consumers read and mutate the **shared** variables `nbElements`, `nbWaitingProd`, and `nbWaitingConso` (and pass the baton between roles). Without a single shared `mutex`, concurrent `nbElements++` and `nbElements--` cause data races, corrupt counts, and lost wakeups.

blocks.title: Exercise 1: Swapping `acquire()` vs. `release()` in BufferNa
blocks.front: In `BufferNa`, what happens if you swap the order of (a) the two `release()` calls at the end, vs. (b) the two `acquire()` calls at the start?
blocks.back:
* **(a) Swapping `release()` calls (`mutex.release()` first):** **Safe & slightly better!** `mutex` is already unlocked when the woken thread resumes.
* **(b) Swapping `acquire()` calls (`mutex.acquire()` first):** **DEADLOCK!** A producer blocking on `waitNotFull.acquire()` while holding `mutex` prevents any consumer from entering `get()` to free a slot.
blocks.hint: Hold-and-wait on `mutex` while blocking on a condition semaphore.

blocks.title: Synthesis: Why `mutexProd` + `mutexConso` Works in BufferNa but Fails in BufferN
blocks.prompt: Explain in your own words which variables are shared between producers and consumers in `BufferNa` versus `BufferN`, and why that determines whether `mutex` can be split into `mutexProd` and `mutexConso`.
self_check_criteria: Stated that in `BufferNa`, `writePointer` is producer-only and `readPointer` is consumer-only.
Explained that in `BufferNa`, `waitNotFull` and `waitNotEmpty` prevent a producer and consumer from touching the same `elements[i]` slot simultaneously.
Stated that in `BufferN`, both producers and consumers read/write `nbElements`, `nbWaitingProd`, and `nbWaitingConso`, making a single shared `mutex` mandatory.
blocks.model_answer: In `BufferNa`, `writePointer` is accessed only by producers and `readPointer` only by consumers, while `waitNotFull`/`waitNotEmpty` ensure they never access the same array index concurrently. Thus `mutexProd` and `mutexConso` suffice and even allow parallel `put()` and `get()`. In `BufferN`, both roles share and mutate `nbElements`, `nbWaitingProd`, and `nbWaitingConso` (and transfer the baton), so a single `mutex` is strictly required.

blocks.question: In `BufferNa::put()`, what is the effect of swapping `waitNotEmpty.release()` and `mutex.release()` so that `mutex.release()` comes first?
options: It is completely valid and slightly better: if a woken consumer runs immediately, `mutex` is already free.
It causes a deadlock when the buffer is full.
It causes a race condition on `writePointer`.
It violates FIFO ordering when multiple consumers are waiting.
blocks.correct_answer: It is completely valid and slightly better: if a woken consumer runs immediately, `mutex` is already free.
blocks.explanation: Once `elements[writePointer]` and `writePointer` have been updated, releasing `mutex` before `waitNotEmpty.release()` is safe and avoids waking a consumer only for it to immediately block on `mutex.acquire()`. (By contrast, swapping the leading `acquire()` calls at the top of `put()`/`get()` WOULD cause a deadlock.)
hints: If `waitNotEmpty.release()` wakes a consumer immediately, what is the next line that consumer executes?

blocks.question: Can we replace the single `mutex` in `BufferNa` and `BufferN` with two separate semaphores (`mutexProd` for producers and `mutexConso` for consumers)?
options: Yes in `BufferNa` (separate `writePointer` and `readPointer`), but NO in `BufferN` (both share `nbElements`, `nbWaitingProd`, and `nbWaitingConso`).
Yes in both `BufferNa` and `BufferN`.
No in `BufferNa`, but yes in `BufferN`.
No in either `BufferNa` or `BufferN`.
blocks.correct_answer: Yes in `BufferNa` (separate `writePointer` and `readPointer`), but NO in `BufferN` (both share `nbElements`, `nbWaitingProd`, and `nbWaitingConso`).
blocks.explanation: In `BufferNa`, `waitNotFull` and `waitNotEmpty` ensure producers and consumers never touch the same array slot simultaneously, and `writePointer`/`readPointer` are disjoint. In `BufferN`, both roles mutate `nbElements`, `nbWaitingProd`, and `nbWaitingConso`, requiring a single shared `mutex`.
hints: Which variables do producers and consumers both modify in `BufferNa` vs. `BufferN`?
In `BufferN`, what happens if a producer increments `nbElements` while a consumer decrements `nbElements`?
